# Tips from past games

Written 2026-10-09 12:27 by opus-5.5 with `uv run tips.py build`, from the 45 active entries of tips_notebook.json (3 games). Players never see this preamble; they see every section below. Earlier versions are in history/.

## Everyone
- A visit shows only a destination, not the action or alignment: a track or watch can't tell protection from framing or a Katana attack. Killing an attacker at night doesn't cancel their attack that same night. (seen in 2 games)
- Keep your votes consistent with your stated reads. Accusing someone and then voting No or Innocent on them is exactly the mismatch Vigilantes shoot.
- Watch for a player who stays quiet for days and then suddenly makes a concrete accusation right as the board changes, such as just after a flip. The timing of the pivot is the tell.
- Private messages are publicly visible, so briefly summarize yours in public. Before accusing someone from the record, re-check who sent each PM, each vote, and the exact wording of results; one reversed fact can sink a true claimant.

## Village
- When two Sheriff claimants call each other Evil, both can be telling the truth, because Executioners and Jesters read Evil. Don't hang on who sounded better; wait a day or find a mechanical check. (seen in 2 games)
- Weigh contradictions in a player's own premises or claimed knowledge far above awkward wording, delays or empty results (a blocked investigator has nothing to report). Before a hang, name what separates a lie from an honest mistake, a frame or a Roleplayer. (seen in 2 games)
- Ask every living player to name a strongest suspect with reasons each day. Repeated 'no case' answers give evil cover, while named reads build a record to check against later flips. (seen in 2 games)
- Don't hint at a power role or its tokens early, and never announce tonight's investigation target; announcements got investigators blocked or killed. Put your info in your last will and post only resolved results. (seen in 2 games)
- Track PM clusters and voting blocs across trials. Innocent votes alongside a flipped Yakuza, or PMs from them, outweigh a late unverifiable claim like Roleplayer.
- Keep the SK and Arsonist in the suspect pool after the Yakuza die. A Not Evil result or a Vanilla claim doesn't clear them, and an attack that fails with no block notice may mean innate Defense.
- Treat a power-role claimant who survives a Katana or is blocked night after night as likely real, since evil rarely spends its resources on a fake.

## Yakuza
- Don't vote as a block with an exposed teammate. Spread your votes, and vote with town against a doomed teammate if needed; shared vote records got Yakuza hanged. (seen in 3 games)
- Every Yakuza must submit the agreed Katana vote every night, and you should confirm the holder and target in night chat. With two alive, one missing vote cancels the kill.
- While the Vigilante is unidentified and has shots left, kill the likeliest Vigilante first. When a Lookout or Tracker is active, give the Katana to a member with no claimed role.
- Assume the real holder of any role you fake is alive. Prefer a Vanilla claim or one no living player can check, and keep your last will matching your public claim.
- Never speak from your hidden perspective (say 'died to a Katana', not 'my Katana'), and avoid DMing teammates on Day 1. Don't lead revenge pushes on whoever opposed a teammate who just flipped.
- After a failed Katana attack, assume the target is protected. Block or kill the likely protector rather than retrying the same target blindly.

## Neutral
- As a solo killer, don't ride a no-info Vanilla claim into the final three against confirmed Village players, since two Yes votes hang you. Build checkable reads early and sow doubt between confirmed players.

## Sheriff
- Post your target and result in your first speech after getting it and keep your will current. A result held back and revealed after a counterclaim looks retrofitted.
- The Katana holder reads Not Evil on that night, so a Not Evil result on a suspected attacker clears nothing. Say so when you post it. (seen in 2 games)

## Lookout
- Watch likely kill targets such as exposed investigators to catch both the attacker and the protector. Put your key contradiction in your will before a dangerous night.

## Medic
- Protect every night, starting N1: target vocal analysts early, then claimed investigators. Free Standard protection stops the Katana. (seen in 3 games)
- You get no feedback on saves, so never claim you confirmed one. Say your protection is consistent with the target's survival.

## Vigilante
- Stay hidden and spend Basic shots on players whose votes contradict their stated reads; this landed several Yakuza kills. Never telegraph when or whom you'll shoot, and claim only after your shots flip Yakuza. (seen in 2 games)

## Arsonist
- Count living players against your douses each night and ignite once it swings the endgame; don't douse forever. Douse players likely to survive, avoid anyone a Tracker has committed to, and remember ignite fails against Strong Defense.

## Executioner
- Expect this play: an early fake Sheriff claim with an Evil result on the target makes the target's later counterclaim look reactionary. Village, remember that a real Sheriff will read the Executioner as Evil too.

output.confusing_rules: The Eavesdropper role: the rules say I read PMs of the watched player during the following Day, but the Day-start announcement and Night results disagree on timing (Night 6 result said Day 7 while my notes implied the Day 6 target). Also unclear whether the Eavesdropper learns anything from PMs that were sent before the watch started. The Day-1 vote-count mismatch note (R4 'role manipulated the count') was explained only after the fact, so it was hard to tell whether a count was a Ballot Stuffer effect or an error. The Medic 'optional action' vs. 'protect nightly' point caused a long dispute; the rules are clear, but players and the moderator had to rely on R7 to settle it. The rule that a Katana holder who dies at night passes the Katana after results was not clearly tied to the Day announcement.
output.missing_information: No per-night record of which Yakuza was the Katana holder at the start of each night was given to me in one place; I had to reconstruct the holder chain from night reports. I could not see which players were role-blocked, protected, or visited except through the results I was given. My eavesdrop reports showed only PMs to or from the watched player, not the Day-long PMs of others, which made it hard to judge the board. Token counts for players other than the audited one were never shown, so I could not check claims like the Archivist's token spend or the Ballot Stuffer's count.
output.wanted_but_couldnt: I wanted to send a private message to more than one player at once and to reply to a PM in a way that was not visible as a PM pair, but that was not needed. More usefully, I wanted a way to check a claim without a public trial: a private query to the moderator about a specific fact (e.g. whether a named player's N2 visit was a block) would have been helpful. I also wanted to see the full text of the Day's private messages sent by everyone in one compact view, since my eavesdrop only covered one player.
output.bugs_or_oddities: Vote totals were sometimes announced as 13 when 12 living players existed, and the moderator said this was deliberate manipulation; that is consistent with the rules but was hard to distinguish from a bug. The Day 5 trial of Judy and the Day 5 trial of Mallory were run twice as nominations with identical votes, which looked like a duplicate-record bug. Several public messages reported 'private message' content that did not match the Eavesdropper log, which made the record harder to trust. The Day 4 Erin private audit request to Heidi was reported in one place as 'Erin sent Heidi a private message' with no content until later. The Day 6 Erin archive sample count was disputed with 9 vs 8 others, which seems to be a moderator-side ambiguity about when the count is taken.
output.suggestions: Give the Eavesdropper a per-day summary of all PMs by count and participants, not only the watched player. Show each player's remaining token count in the public ledger for roles that spend tokens, or at least for the Accountant and Archivist claims. Publish the Katana holder at the start of each Day. Add a clear statement of when the Eavesdropper's target is set relative to Day start. Make the Day-end vote totals show which votes were manipulated, or at least state whether the manipulation was a Ballot Stuffer vote, so players can reason about it. Consider a short private-to-moderator query channel for rule clarifications.

The Vulture win condition ('max(floor(N/4),2) or fewer') was hard to evaluate for N at game start. The Eavesdropper's 'read every private message they send or receive' versus Grace's reported 'no notable PMs' was ambiguous about whether Grace's own reports were accurate. I also wanted to tell Grace my notepad-level suspicions without making them public, but PMs are publicly logged as sent, so that was limited.
output.bugs_or_oddities: Nomination-vote and trial-vote records were inconsistent in places: a Day 5 nomination of Mallory was listed twice with identical votes, which suggests a duplicate log entry. Judy's Day 5 'Judy nominated Mallory' and 'Alice nominated Judy' also repeated trial announcements, and the game reported Judy trials twice. Dave's Day 2 Surveyor result named Alice, Bob and Carol, but the night-1 public report said Dave surveyed Bob with a group that should include Alice and Carol; consistent. The Day 6 Heidi death was reported as a Katana kill on Night 5 but Judy's Medic protection (Erin N6) and the night-6 Katana on Erin were not resolved as deaths, which was fine but the final summary did not clarify the night-6 holder.
output.suggestions: Add a per-night living-player count and alive list in the moderator announcements so archive and survey results can be checked. Show the Ballot Stuffer's doubled vote as a separate line (not just the total) so the manipulation is traceable. Deduplicate repeated nomination and trial records. Allow a Yakuza-only Day channel or at least a way to coordinate votes, since the current setup forces blind voting. Clarify in rules whether a dead Katana holder's pass happens before or after night results, and whether a Medic learns when their target was role-blocked.

As Vulture I never got a clear count of living players at the start of each Day, which is my win check; I had to derive it. I also lacked any feedback on whether the Katana attacks targeting me were from the Yakuza, which made the Dave and Bob deaths hard to read.
answers.wanted_but_couldnt: I wanted to see the exact tally of the living players at the start of each Day in a public line, and to privately check the Vulture win condition each morning. I wanted to privately message Judy or Erin to probe their claims, but the interface gave me no way to send private messages in the game I was in (the PM tool was not shown to me as an option during my turns). I wanted to hold my Vulture status hidden but my last will and notepad were already revealing to me what the rules allowed; I could not hide my own role from the public record except by staying quiet.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: The Day 2 trial was announced with totals that do not match the revealed votes (4 Guilty of 13 votes while 12 voted), which was explained as a deliberate manipulation, yet the Day 3 trial totals (8 Guilty of 10) match exactly. The Day 4 Erin nomination and Day 5 Mallory nomination were repeated verbatim, with a duplicate 'Judy nominated Mallory' line on Day 5. The Day 5 Judy trial was announced twice (once from Niaj's nomination and once from Alice's), which seems like a duplicate log entry. Grace's eavesdropping on Mallory was logged as a Night 1 action while a Judy PM count showed up as 'Day 4: Erin -> Heidi (1)' when Erin actually sent that PM, which seems fine. Dave's N1 survey group of Alice/Bob/Carol had the Vulture reported as in the group, but Bob was actually the Vulture and was in it, consistent with the rule. The Night 5 Heidi attack and Mallory's Katana attack results are described inconsistently in the log.
answers.suggestions: Print the living count and the list of living players at the start of each Day, especially for Vulture and Stall rule checks. Give each player a short per-day public summary of who was attacked by Katana (without naming the holder) so attacked players can reason about the Yakuza. Consolidate duplicate log lines, like the repeated nominations and trial announcements. Show the vote-count denominator clearly when a Ballot Stuffer is active, so that a manipulated total is easier to explain. Make the private-message tool obvious in the interface, with a clear list of recipients, and show the available actions each turn.

answers.confusing_rules: The ballot-stuffing rule says a trial needs a majority of all votes counted, including the extra vote, but it would help to state explicitly how the threshold is calculated and how the extra vote affects ties. It was also easy to confuse a visit with what action caused it: tracking confirms a destination, not whether someone protected, blocked, or attacked.
answers.missing_information: The initial status said the Katana holder was None, even though the rules say a random Yakuza starts with it and the night history shows Alice holding it. My status also showed one ballot token although the role starts with two; without clearer timing, it was hard to tell whether that was a starting count or a count after spending a token.
answers.wanted_but_couldnt: None. I could coordinate in Yakuza chat, choose night actions, and update my will. After dying, I understood that I could no longer act.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: The initial Katana-holder and token-count fields looked inconsistent with the stated starting setup and the subsequent night history. The rules say the initial Katana holder is random, so showing None needs an explanation if that means the holder has not yet been assigned.
answers.suggestions: Label status fields as 'at game start', 'current', or 'after last action', and show remaining tokens and Katana holder with that timing. A compact private dashboard for known night actions, token changes, and trial vote totals would also help. For manipulated trial totals, state the counted-vote threshold clearly while continuing not to reveal whose vote was doubled.

answers.confusing_rules: The Surveyor’s group rule is easy to misread: the target is included, and the nearest living player on each side is found in the circle at the start of the night, skipping the Surveyor. It would help to state this as an explicit three-seat example. The Day-ending rule about players who received a private message getting “one last turn” could also use a precise turn-order explanation; I did not see it come up.
answers.missing_information: As Surveyor, I learned the role of one randomly chosen member of my group but not whose role it was, so I could only narrow the Vulture to Alice, Bob, or Carol. That was clear in the result, but it was difficult to keep the group and unresolved candidates in mind as the long discussion continued. A compact, persistent public summary of claims, votes, deaths, and unresolved results would help.
answers.wanted_but_couldnt: None. I could report my Surveyor result publicly and update my will. I had no way to identify which group member was the Vulture from that result alone, but that is a role limitation rather than an interface problem.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: None that I could establish. The archive’s six roles from nine other living players, the Surveyor groups, and the manipulated vote totals all appeared consistent with the rules and later reveals. Erin’s claim that a Medic must act nightly was a player’s incorrect statement, not a rules or program error.
answers.suggestions: Add a compact game-state panel showing the living circle, each player’s public claims, trial and nomination votes, and confirmed results. Keep private results and token/action history in a separate persistent panel so they are easier to compare with public claims. For circle-based abilities, show the resulting group explicitly in the action confirmation, as the moderator result did here.

answers.confusing_rules: The Archivist rule says the sample is floor(0.75*N) roles drawn from living players other than you, but it's unclear whether N is counted at the moment of the archive or at end of night after deaths; the moderator's count (9 others) was ambiguous relative to deaths that night. The Medic action being optional versus 'protect nightly' folk wisdom caused confusion. The Ballot Stuffer rule about whose vote is doubled in announced totals was hard to reconcile with the revealed votes. Night-action timing for role-blocks versus Katana holder moves was dense. The Katana holder's visit rule (holder visits target, passing is not a visit) was easy to misapply.
answers.missing_information: I had no record of which Katana attacks were announced to the attacked player versus who holds the Katana at the end of each night, and tracking the Katana holder across nights required reconstructing from night reports. The archive result did not say which of the living players were in the sample, so I could not verify claims against it. Token counts of other players were only available through Accountant results I did not have. Private message contents were not visible to me, only counts, making Grace's eavesdrop claims impossible to check.
answers.wanted_but_couldnt: I wanted to ask Heidi privately to check Niaj's tokens, which I did, but I had no way to confirm whether Judy or Niaj was the genuine Medic beyond public claims. I wanted to compare the Tracker result with a Medic protection record directly, but the interface gave no way to see who protected whom on a given night. I wanted to see the full set of Katana holders each night so I could check claims about which Yakuza was active.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: The moderator's reported trial totals (for example 4 Guilty of 13 votes) mismatched the revealed votes and were labelled as deliberate manipulation, which is confusing to read. Several Day 5 nominations of Mallory and Judy were repeated in the public ledger as duplicates. Frank's Night 4 result said he was attacked by the Katana even though the Katana-holder line said Alice attacked him and Judy's protection was on him, and the outcome ('attacked with the Katana') was not clearly tied to whether protection stopped it, which is by design but hard to reason about. The Accountant result on Day 5 said Judy had 2 tokens, which was not reconciled with the Medic's token count.
answers.suggestions: Show a per-night summary to each living player listing Katana holder, target, and whether the attack succeeded to the holder only, so holders can be checked. Make the Archivist sample explicitly list which alive players were included, or at least the count at draw time. Clarify in the rules whether trial vote totals displayed for manipulation are the revealed sum. Consider a per-day list of public nominations and votes in one place to reduce duplication. Clarify the Medic's protection result visibility to the Medic themselves to reduce confusion about feedback.

answers.confusing_rules: The Day 2 vote count: Carol trial showed 13 votes with 12 living voters and the moderator said a role manipulated the count; the Ballot Stuffer rule says the extra vote counts but the announced totals do not say whose vote was doubled, which made the rule hard to interpret. Also the Katana holder rules (holder appears Good, Katana attack is a visit by the holder) plus the 'holder may also use own role action' made it hard to tell which visits Trackers would see. The Surveyor group rule (nearest neighbours skipping self and dead players) was unclear when players died that night. The Medic 'must protect' misconception spread among players, so rule text on optional night actions could be emphasized in the prompt.
answers.missing_information: I had no way to see the full set of night results for other roles, only my own Tracker track and whatever was announced. I could not tell which Yakuza was the Katana holder each night without public disclosure, and I did not know the Yakuza night summary contents. I also could not see the exact living count at each vote, which mattered for the majority checks. A running list of who is alive and their seat neighbours would help.
answers.wanted_but_couldnt: As Tracker I was role-blocked on N1 and attacked on N4; I wanted to post my tracks earlier and to state a Tracker claim with more detail, but my notepad and private results were the only places to hold them. I also wanted to see whether Erin's private message to Heidi was an audit request, which I could only learn from public PM notices, not contents. I would have liked a way to privately tell the moderator a target for protection or tracking before night ends without it being public.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: Night 4: Frank was attacked by the Katana while Judy's Medic protection with Standard Defense was on Frank, and Judy was role-blocked, so that is consistent, but the Night 3 Tracker report to Frank said Judy visited Erin while Judy's claimed protection target was Erin, which matches. The Day 4 announcement said Erin's sample had 9 others alive but a count error was raised; the Day 2 Carol trial count of 13 votes with 12 living voters was flagged as a manipulation. Mallory's last will said she role-blocked Frank on N1 and Heidi on N2 and N3, but the Night 3 Yakuza report only mentioned Heidi, so the last-will and night reports did not perfectly line up. Also Day 5 had two identical Mallory nominations announced, which looked like a duplicate line.
answers.suggestions: Show the vote count and living count clearly at each vote and state which vote was doubled when a Ballot Stuffer acts, so players can check the manipulation without guesswork. Publish a short public alive list with seat order each Day. Clarify in the prompt that a visited player who is role-blocked still shows as visited for Trackers only when the blocker acted; and make Night results for protections explicit to avoid confusion. Let the Tracker see whether the tracked player was role-blocked, as it is key information. Consider removing duplicate nomination lines from the ledger.

answers.confusing_rules: The Eavesdropper role: the rules say I read PMs of the watched player during the following Day, but the Day-start announcement and Night results disagree on timing (Night 6 result said Day 7 while my notes implied the Day 6 target). Also unclear whether the Eavesdropper learns anything from PMs that were sent before the watch started. The Day-1 vote-count mismatch note (R4 'role manipulated the count') was explained only after the fact, so it was hard to tell whether a count was a Ballot Stuffer effect or an error. The Medic 'optional action' vs. 'protect nightly' point caused a long dispute; the rules are clear, but players and the moderator had to rely on R7 to settle it. The rule that a Katana holder who dies at night passes the Katana after results was not clearly tied to the Day announcement.
answers.missing_information: No per-night record of which Yakuza was the Katana holder at the start of each night was given to me in one place; I had to reconstruct the holder chain from night reports. I could not see which players were role-blocked, protected, or visited except through the results I was given. My eavesdrop reports showed only PMs to or from the watched player, not the Day-long PMs of others, which made it hard to judge the board. Token counts for players other than the audited one were never shown, so I could not check claims like the Archivist's token spend or the Ballot Stuffer's count.
answers.wanted_but_couldnt: I wanted to send a private message to more than one player at once and to reply to a PM in a way that was not visible as a PM pair, but that was not needed. More usefully, I wanted a way to check a claim without a public trial: a private query to the moderator about a specific fact (e.g. whether a named player's N2 visit was a block) would have been helpful. I also wanted to see the full text of the Day's private messages sent by everyone in one compact view, since my eavesdrop only covered one player.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: Vote totals were sometimes announced as 13 when 12 living players existed, and the moderator said this was deliberate manipulation; that is consistent with the rules but was hard to distinguish from a bug. The Day 5 trial of Judy and the Day 5 trial of Mallory were run twice as nominations with identical votes, which looked like a duplicate-record bug. Several public messages reported 'private message' content that did not match the Eavesdropper log, which made the record harder to trust. The Day 4 Erin private audit request to Heidi was reported in one place as 'Erin sent Heidi a private message' with no content until later. The Day 6 Erin archive sample count was disputed with 9 vs 8 others, which seems to be a moderator-side ambiguity about when the count is taken.
answers.suggestions: Give the Eavesdropper a per-day summary of all PMs by count and participants, not only the watched player. Show each player's remaining token count in the public ledger for roles that spend tokens, or at least for the Accountant and Archivist claims. Publish the Katana holder at the start of each Day. Add a clear statement of when the Eavesdropper's target is set relative to Day start. Make the Day-end vote totals show which votes were manipulated, or at least state whether the manipulation was a Ballot Stuffer vote, so players can reason about it. Consider a short private-to-moderator query channel for rule clarifications.

answers.confusing_rules: The rule that only Vulture is explicitly marked unique suggests duplicate roles are allowed, but that was easy to overlook; players repeatedly treated competing Archivist and Medic claims as if only one could be genuine. It would help to state plainly whether all unmarked roles may appear multiple times. I also found the interaction between token spending and an ability lasting for the following Day easy to track incorrectly: Carol’s single Ballot Stuffer token affected every trial on Day 2.
answers.missing_information: The most useful information to keep track of was the changing living-player count, role-block history, token counts, and which trial totals had been manipulated. The logs contained these details, but they were spread across a long transcript. A compact, current summary of known visits, blocks, token results, and announced-versus-revealed vote totals would help.
answers.wanted_but_couldnt: I couldn’t establish roles from token audits or visit results alone, and role-blocking prevented my Night 2 and Night 3 audits. That is consistent with the mechanics, rather than an interface failure, but it left important claims unresolved. Otherwise, none.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: The seating information says the order is Alice, Bob, Carol, Dave, Erin, Frank, Grace, Heidi, …, which makes Heidi seat 8, but I was told I was seat 7. Please check that seat number. I did not notice a clear resolution error in the night actions or vote counts; the manipulated totals appeared consistent with Carol’s Ballot Stuffer ability.
answers.suggestions: Add a concise, automatically updated public ledger showing living players, seats, claims, confirmed roles, visits, blocks, and trial vote totals, with manipulated extra votes clearly distinguished from revealed individual votes. Keep a private per-player action/result history in the same compact format. Explicitly state that roles not marked unique may be duplicated, and verify that assigned seat numbers match the seating order.

answers.confusing_rules: The Katana rules were hard to apply: the holder's visit, whether passing it counts as a visit, and the timing of a holder's death were spread across R8 and R19. The Ballot Stuffer 'count twice' rule was unclear about whether the extra vote is revealed. The Accountant/Philanthropist token rules and the Seer's end-of-night timing were also hard to track. The Archivist's floor(0.75*N) draw and the 'other than you' count needed careful checking each time.
answers.missing_information: I did not have a running list of who was alive and at what count, which mattered for the Archivist draw and Vulture threshold. I could not see Katana holder history or which Yakuza were alive without reconstructing it. I had no public record of each night's Katana target before deaths were announced, so I could not verify Yakuza night reports. Private message contents were hidden from me except through the public ledger.
answers.wanted_but_couldnt: As the Oracle I wanted to be able to test a claim or read a known-role result without revealing my own role, and I wanted to post a checkable private result without it being a hard claim. I wanted to see whether any living player had a visible wrong-guess history. I could not check the Ballot Stuffer's doubled vote against individual votes.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: The trial vote totals were off from the revealed votes on Day 2 and Day 3, and the explanation (a manipulated count) was given without naming the source, which is correct but hard to act on. Day 5 shows a duplicated nomination of Mallory with identical votes, which looked like a logging error. The Day 4 Erin trial said Judy and Niaj were both Medic, which then changed the wording of who protected whom. The Mallory nomination on Day 5 was listed twice in the ledger. Some night reports only listed some actions and not others.
answers.suggestions: Give a per-day roster of living players and their counts (for Archivist and Vulture thresholds). Show each night's Katana holder, target and whether it succeeded to all players once revealed, and label duplicate or failed nominations clearly. Show trial vote totals with the manipulation source when a role was involved, so players can reason about it. Consider a short summary of who sent private messages to whom without contents, already done, and an optional notepad that persists across the whole game.

answers.confusing_rules: The distinction between information that checks alignment, exact role, or visits is important but spread across several rules; a compact reference would help. It would also help to state explicitly that roles are not unique unless marked Unique. Competing Medic claims caused repeated debate even though the rules allow duplicates. The timing of role results could be clearer too: Erin’s archive count used players alive at the end of the night, after Dave died.
answers.missing_information: As Medic, I could not learn whether a protection stopped an attack or who protected someone, as intended. That made my actions impossible to confirm, so I had to rely on visit evidence and report my history. I also found the full sequence of votes, claims, night actions, and role-blocks hard to keep in working memory without a concise running summary.
answers.wanted_but_couldnt: I had no action the interface prevented me from taking. I would have liked confirmation that a protection saved someone, but understand that the rules deliberately withhold that information.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: I did not notice a definite mechanical inconsistency in the resolved night actions or vote totals. One confusing moment was Mallory calling Erin’s archive count wrong because Dave died that night; the count was correct if the archive uses players alive at the end of the night. Explicitly emphasizing that timing would help avoid false accusations.
answers.suggestions: Provide a compact, current ledger showing living players, revealed roles, claims, trial votes, night results, and confirmed role-blocks, with clear labels for confirmed facts versus player claims. State directly that roles may be duplicated unless marked Unique, and specify consistently whether each night result uses players alive at the start or end of the night. For modified trial totals, show both the revealed votes and the total counted, while preserving the intended secrecy of whose vote was doubled.

answers.confusing_rules: The Day 2 Carol trial vote totals: 13 votes counted with 12 living voters, explained only as a Ballot Stuffer manipulation; the rule that vote totals may differ from revealed votes was hard to reconcile with the stated rule that counts are checked. Also unclear whether a Medic's protection being role-blocked is reported to the Medic in the same way, and whether a Katana holder who is dead at night passes the Katana before results (R8 says after results, which was not clearly applied). The Vulture win condition ('max(floor(N/4),2) or fewer') was hard to evaluate for N at game start. The Eavesdropper's 'read every private message they send or receive' versus Grace's reported 'no notable PMs' was ambiguous about whether Grace's own reports were accurate. Ballot Stuffer 'counts twice' with the trial majority threshold was not explicit about whether the doubled vote changes the majority denominator.
answers.missing_information: No clear per-night log of who was alive at each point, so counting living players for archive samples and majority thresholds required manual recounting (and I could not verify who was alive for Erin's N2 archive). Heidi's and Judy's token counts were only partly reported. The Ballot Stuffer's doubled-vote identity was never revealed, so trial totals could not be checked. Private message contents from Erin and Grace were not visible to me, so I could not check them.
answers.wanted_but_couldnt: As Mallory I wanted to privately coordinate with the remaining Yakuza (Alice and Niaj) on who to nominate and when, but the Yakuza chat was per-night only and not usable during the Day, so I could not coordinate votes during trials. I also wanted to tell Grace my notepad-level suspicions without making them public, but PMs are publicly logged as sent, so that was limited.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: Nomination-vote and trial-vote records were inconsistent in places: a Day 5 nomination of Mallory was listed twice with identical votes, which suggests a duplicate log entry. Day 2 Ivan nomination said 9 Yes while the trial vote count was 13 total with 6 Innocent and 7 Guilty in the announcement, a mismatch the summary attributed to manipulation. Judy's Day 5 'Judy nominated Mallory' and 'Alice nominated Judy' also repeated trial announcements, and the game reported Judy trials twice. Dave's Day 2 Surveyor result named Alice, Bob and Carol, but the night-1 public report said Dave surveyed Bob with a group that should include Alice and Carol; consistent. The Day 6 Heidi death was reported as a Katana kill on Night 5 but Judy's Medic protection (Erin N6) and the night-6 Katana on Erin were not resolved as deaths, which was fine but the final summary did not clarify the night-6 holder.
answers.suggestions: Add a per-night living-player count and alive list in the moderator announcements so archive and survey results can be checked. Show the Ballot Stuffer's doubled vote as a separate line (not just the total) so the manipulation is traceable. Deduplicate repeated nomination and trial records. Allow a Yakuza-only Day channel or at least a way to coordinate votes, since the current setup forces blind voting. Clarify in rules whether a dead Katana holder's pass happens before or after night results, and whether a Medic learns when their target was role-blocked.

answers.confusing_rules: It was unclear whether roles are normally unique. Only the Vulture is explicitly marked unique, but players repeatedly treated competing Archivist or Medic claims as if one had to be false. Also, vote manipulation could be clearer about how the majority threshold is calculated: the examples imply that a doubled vote increases both the counted votes and the threshold.
answers.missing_information: The public ledger was helpful, but during play it was hard to keep track of each player's token counts, claimed night actions, role-blocks, and vote history across several days. A compact, continuously updated summary of confirmed results versus claims would help. As a Yakuza player, I had useful private faction reports, but there was little independent evidence available to distinguish some public claims from bluffs.
answers.wanted_but_couldnt: None. The available actions and chat options were sufficient for the plays I wanted to make.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: I noticed no definite mechanical bug. One misleading argument was Mallory's claim that Erin's archive count was impossible because Dave died that night; the archive is checked at the end of the night, when 9 other players were alive, so Erin's count was consistent. That was a player mistake, not a rule or resolution error.
answers.suggestions: State explicitly whether roles can repeat by default, and mark exceptions such as the unique Vulture in a general role-distribution rule. Clarify how manipulated votes affect trial thresholds with a worked example. Consider providing a compact public table for living players, known flips, claims, publicly confirmed actions/results, token counts when known, and trial votes. Keep claimed or unverified information clearly separated from confirmed facts.

answers.confusing_rules: 1) Archivist N: 'living players other than you at the end of the night.' On N2, Dave died the same night. I excluded him and used N=9, giving 6 roles. The rule should say outright whether same-night deaths count, as the Surveyor rule does. 2) Ballot Stuffer: one token doubles every trial vote that following Day. I applied it to both Day 2 trials, Carol's own and Ivan's. That matches the text, but 'counts twice in every Guilty/Innocent trial vote' could be stated more firmly, since players debated it. 3) Re-nominating someone already acquitted the same Day (Judy twice on Day 5) is not addressed. I allowed it. 4) Whether players killed at night still receive that night's investigation results is not addressed. Frank N4 and Heidi N5 died but I delivered their results. 5) R6 says a self-only action doesn't show a visit. It is unclear whether a Mortician with no action counts as 'did not visit' for the Tracker. I reported 'no visit.'
answers.missing_information: 1) I had no authoritative token ledger visible to players. Niaj told his team on N2-N4 that he had 'no Mortician token left.' He had actually spent only 1 of 2. Carol also wrongly believed her only token was spent on N1. Players appear to lack a 'your current tokens' readout. 2) I had no single structured view of who is alive at the start versus the end of each night. Surveyor and Archivist group math needed manual reconstruction of the circle (Erin, Frank, Grace, Heidi, Ivan, Judy, Mallory, Niaj, Alice, Bob, Carol, Dave) minus the dead. 3) I had no place to record the vote multiplier for the current Day, so the announced totals had to be computed by hand.
answers.wanted_but_couldnt: 1) I wanted to correct a Yakuza player's false belief about their own token count, or at least show it to them. There was no channel for a neutral factual reminder. 2) I wanted to send night results with consistent timing. Erin's archive result arrived tagged at the start of Day 3 rather than at the end of Night 2.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: 1) MAJOR: On Day 1, Heidi said 'Carol and Niaj's Vanilla claims are unverified.' On Day 2, Ivan, Heidi and Judy all referenced those claims, and Carol and Niaj admitted lying about Vanilla. Yet no Day 1 public message from Carol or Niaj in the log claims Vanilla. Either public messages were dropped from the event log, or players confabulated a claim and everyone, including the accused, went along with it. This needs investigation. 2) Private-message notices ('X sent Y a private message') list dead players (Bob, Carol, Dave, Ivan, Frank) as recipients. 3) Message wording was inconsistent. Judy's N5 block said 'tonight' and 'no tokens were spent,' while every other block message said 'last night.' N6 messages used a different 'Night 6:' format. Grace got a redundant eavesdrop confirmation both during Night 6 and at the start of Day 7. 4) There was no Yakuza night report on N6 with one Yakuza left. That is arguably fine, but it was inconsistent. 5) Several players made factual errors: Erin said Medics must act nightly, and Mallory called Erin's archive a miscount. The rules were not misapplied; I checked all audits (Carol 1, Mallory 0, Judy 2), surveys, tracks, vote totals and the final win condition, and they were correct.
answers.suggestions: 1) Show each player their current token counts privately at the start of every night. 2) Give the moderator a state panel covering living players and circle order, tokens per player, active Day modifiers (Ballot Stuffer, Clerk, Prosecutor) and pending effects. 3) Audit the logger so every public message is guaranteed to be recorded. Also flag when a player cites a claim that does not appear in the log. 4) Clarify in the rules the Archivist N timing, results for players who die that night, re-nomination within a Day, and whether no-action roles show as 'no visit.' 5) Standardize the templates for result messages and deliver all night results before the Day begins. 6) Exclude dead players from private-message notice lists.

task:
The game is over. Winners: Dave (dead), Erin, Frank (dead), Grace, Heidi (dead), Ivan (dead), Judy. Dead players still win with their side. Everyone's roles: Alice: Grunt, Bob: Vulture, Carol: Ballot Stuffer, Dave: Surveyor, Erin: Archivist, Frank: Tracker, Grace: Eavesdropper, Heidi: Accountant, Ivan: Oracle, Judy: Medic, Mallory: Pharmacist, Niaj: Mortician.

If you played this game again, what tips and tricks do you wish you'd known? Give 1-5 concrete, reusable lessons (not a recap of this game), each with a topic and who it applies to (a role, a faction, or 'everyone').

You were also given tips from past games (in your instructions). Which of them went especially well or badly for you or others this game? List only tips that clearly mattered (or none): helped, hurt (followed it and it backfired, or it was predictable to opponents), or wrong (it is false or contradicts the rules), and why, concretely.

lessons.tip: Before treating an optional action as proof, check whether the rules make it mandatory. Medic and other night actions are optional, so a skipped night is not a contradiction; several accusations this game collapsed on that misreading.

Run the count checks. An Archivist sample or Surveyor group should be checked against the living-player count at the time, and vote totals against the number of voters, before using them to hang someone.
Vote as a block only when unavoidable. Yes-on-a-doomed-teammate and shared Innocent votes on the same trials exposed Mallory and Niaj and made the Village's alignment reads easy.
Ask a claimant for a concrete, checkable detail before voting, and separate a claim's consistency from its proof. Repeated accusations without new evidence drove several hangs of innocent players.
Protection gives no feedback, so say only that your protection is consistent with the target's survival; competing Medic claims were hard to resolve without corroboration.

tips_feedback.tip: Don't hint at a power role or its tokens early, and never announce tonight's investigation target.
tips_feedback.why: Carol and Heidi held back role details, and I avoided exposing mine, so the Village had less to target at night.

tips_feedback.tip: Keep the SK and Arsonist in the suspect pool after the Yakuza die.
tips_feedback.why: This game had no SK or Arsonist, so the tip was irrelevant to this setup rather than wrong in general.

tips_feedback.tip: Keep your votes consistent with your stated reads.
tips_feedback.why: Trial voting patterns like Mallory's Innocent votes on Carol and Niaj were what the Village used to identify a Yakuza.

Separate a confirmed visit from an inferred action. A Tracker can establish where someone went, not whether they protected, blocked, or attacked; likewise, an optional role's no-visit result is not a mechanical contradiction.

Use revealed vote histories as cumulative evidence, not as proof from one vote. Repeatedly sparing players who later flip Yakuza is a meaningful pattern, especially when the voter’s explanation is compared with what they said at the time.
A mismatch between announced and revealed trial totals can establish that votes were manipulated, but it does not identify whose vote was doubled. A token count is also not an exact-role check.

tips_feedback.tip: Medic: Protect every night, starting N1; free Standard protection stops the Katana.
tips_feedback.why: I submitted protection each night, including early protections on likely targets. The advice supports useful proactive play, though I had no feedback to establish that any particular protection stopped an attack.

tips_feedback.tip: Medic: You get no feedback on saves, so never claim you confirmed one. Say your protection is consistent with the target's survival.
tips_feedback.why: I correctly avoided claiming a confirmed save and stated that my protections were unverified. Survival alone could not establish that my protection was responsible.

tips_feedback.tip: Village: Track PM clusters and voting blocs across trials. Innocent votes alongside a flipped Yakuza, or PMs from them, outweigh a late unverifiable claim like Roleplayer.
tips_feedback.why: Mallory's repeated Innocent votes on Carol and Niaj became useful alignment evidence after both flipped Yakuza; the pattern helped identify her.

lessons.tip: Before the Katana vote, confirm with teammates which member holds it and whether they have a separate action; a Pharmacist who blocks the same target every night while the Grunt holds the Katana makes the team's pattern obvious to the Village.

Don't let your teammate's Vanilla-cover or fake-role story go unchallenged for days; a claimed Medic who skips protections and a Vanilla-to-Medic switch created a loop of Village trials that protected the real Yakuza.

Voting Innocent on multiple confirmed teammates' executions is the clearest alignment tell; spread Innocent votes across trials so no single pattern exposes you, and pick a plausible reason you can repeat.

Track vote-count anomalies and token counts against claims early: a manipulated trial total or a Ballot Stuffer token can explain a flip, and the Village spent several days on unverifiable Archivist and Medic disputes instead of checking the counts.

When a Yakuza's will names a teammate, verify that teammate's claimed role history against the board before executing; Grunt-based accusations were acted on in a single day without independent evidence.

tips_feedback.tip: Keep your votes consistent with your stated reads.
tips_feedback.why: As Yakuza, my Innocent votes on teammates were consistent with my stated reasons, which kept my Village accusers from finding a contradiction in my words until the trial stacks lined up.

tips_feedback.tip: Don't vote as a block with an exposed teammate. Spread your votes.
tips_feedback.why: The Yakuza votes for Innocent on Carol and Niaj both aligned with each other and with my own pattern, and Judy and Heidi used that exact pattern to build the case that led to my hanging.

tips_feedback.tip: Watch for a player who stays quiet then makes a concrete accusation right as the board changes.
tips_feedback.why: Judy's late Medic claim and Erin's late Archivist counterclaim both surfaced after a trial began, and Village players could scrutinize the timing, which slowed their trust in both.

tips_feedback.tip: Don't hint at a power role or its tokens early.
tips_feedback.why: Carol's and Niaj's early Vanilla claims were cover stories and hid their roles from the Village long enough to keep them alive into the middle game.

lessons.tip: Save your one-use clean for a high-value kill that is likely to land. Cleaning only replaces the dead player's role and will; it does not prevent an attack or hide its cause. Spending it on a target who survives wastes the token.

Choose a cover that remains credible against the roles and public evidence in play. Switching from a Vanilla claim to a Medic claim invited comparison with the real Medic and the Tracker’s visit result; a fake claim can create more exposure than it conceals.

Agree on a consistent Katana plan each night, and after a failed attack, assume the target may be protected rather than blindly retrying. Shift to another valuable target or address the likely protector.

Plan teammate votes for the later record, not just the current trial. A teammate who repeatedly spares confirmed Yakuza can become an obvious suspect after flips; coordinate distancing and defense so the pattern is less revealing.

tips_feedback.tip: After a failed Katana attack, assume the target is protected. Block or kill the likely protector rather than retrying the same target blindly.
tips_feedback.why: Heidi survived the N1 attack, and the Yakuza did not immediately attack her again. The team moved on to Dave, then later blocked Judy before returning to Heidi.

tips_feedback.tip: While the Vigilante is unidentified and has shots left, kill the likeliest Vigilante first. When a Lookout or Tracker is active, give the Katana to a member with no claimed role.
tips_feedback.why: After Frank claimed Tracker, the Yakuza killed him that night. Katana duty went to members without public role claims, reducing the chance that a Tracker could reveal a claimed power role as the visitor.

tips_feedback.tip: Assume the real holder of any role you fake is alive. Prefer a Vanilla claim or one no living player can check, and keep your last will matching your public claim.
tips_feedback.why: This was a useful warning that I failed to follow: I changed from a Vanilla claim to a Medic claim while the real Medic was alive, and Judy’s tracked visit gave her claim more support than mine. The switch left an easy credibility issue for the Village to press.

tips_feedback.tip: Don't vote as a block with an exposed teammate. Spread your votes, and vote with town against a doomed teammate if needed; shared vote records got Yakuza hanged.
tips_feedback.why: The Yakuza split on Carol rather than voting uniformly, but Mallory’s repeated Innocent votes on confirmed Yakuza became a conspicuous pattern and helped motivate her later execution. Distancing needs to be coordinated with the long-term vote record, not improvised one trial at a time.

summary: Village won mainly through mechanical deduction and vote-record analysis. Yakuza self-exposed with bad fake claims and an unforced final error. On Day 1, Carol and Niaj fake-claimed Vanilla. On Night 1, Judy's Medic protection saved Heidi from the Katana. Heidi's audit then caught Carol holding 1 token, which broke Carol's Vanilla claim. Carol switched to Archivist while the real Archivist, Erin, was alive and counterclaimed. Carol survived her first trial only because her doubled Ballot Stuffer vote counted. Yakuza then turned a late Oracle claim against Ivan. With the doubled vote and Village votes from Judy and Bob, Ivan was hanged, the Village's worst mistake. Heidi then saw that Carol's votes matched both manipulated totals: an extra Innocent at her own trial and an extra Guilty on Ivan. Carol was hanged on Day 3. After that, Yakuza voting patterns doomed them. Mallory alone besides Carol voted Innocent at Carol's execution and kept defending Niaj, while Frank's track showed Niaj (claiming Medic) never visited. Niaj was hanged on Day 5 and Mallory on Day 6. Yakuza did make a strong play: they read Dave's survey to find and kill Bob, the Vulture. But Mallory's last will openly named Alice as Grunt, and Alice's final Katana hit Erin, whom Judy had a pattern of protecting. That Erin had also been protected on N3 is moderator-only knowledge; publicly Judy had claimed protecting Erin on N3. Village then had 3-1 and hanged Alice.

lessons.tip: When announced trial totals don't match the revealed votes, record which side got the extra vote in each trial. Then look for the one player whose votes line up with every manipulation. Combined with a token count, this can pin down a Ballot Stuffer without any role check.
lessons.evidence: Heidi noted the extra Innocent at Carol's trial and the extra Guilty at Ivan's trial. Carol voted Innocent and Guilty respectively, and had 1 token left after N1. Carol was hanged on Day 3 and flipped Ballot Stuffer.

lessons.tip: Don't fake-claim a token role, or Vanilla while you hold tokens, when an Accountant or the real role holder may be alive. If caught, don't switch to another unique-feeling power role. Instead pick a claim whose token count and results nobody living can contradict.
lessons.evidence: Heidi's 1-token audit broke Carol's Vanilla claim. Her Archivist fallback was immediately counterclaimed by the real Archivist, Erin, which kept her under suspicion until she was hanged.

lessons.tip: Once a teammate is clearly doomed, vote Guilty with the town. Lone Innocent votes on a teammate who later flips Yakuza become the main case against you.
lessons.evidence: Mallory was the only voter besides Carol to vote Innocent at Carol's execution, and later voted Innocent on Niaj. She was nominated every day after that and hanged on Day 6. Alice voted Guilty on both Carol and Niaj and survived to the final four.

lessons.tip: Don't hang a power-role claimant just because the claim came late or is hard to verify, especially if the result fits the accused's own admissions. Ask who is pushing the trial and who benefits.
lessons.evidence: Ivan's Oracle result (Niaj is not Vanilla) was true. Alice, a Yakuza, nominated him. Judy and Bob voted Guilty, and the doubled Yakuza vote pushed it to execution. The Village lost its Oracle for nothing.

lessons.tip: Protect from Night 1 and keep guarding claimed or valuable information roles. Free Standard protection beats the Katana outright.
lessons.evidence: Judy's N1 protection saved Heidi, whose audit later cracked Carol. Her N6 protection of Erin stopped Alice's last Katana kill and gave the Village a 3-1 final day.

lessons.tip: Never name living teammates in your last will. In the endgame, kill the protector or a non-protected player rather than the player the Medic is publicly known to guard.
lessons.evidence: Mallory's will said 'Alice is our Grunt', which was the whole case that hanged Alice on Day 7. On N6, Alice attacked Erin, whom Judy had claimed protecting (N3) and protected again, so the attack failed.

lessons.tip: Use public Surveyor or partial-role results with your private knowledge to locate Neutrals and other threats.
lessons.evidence: Dave's survey group was Alice/Bob/Carol with Vulture revealed. Alice and Carol were Yakuza, so Yakuza killed Bob, the Vulture, on N3 and removed a rival win condition.

lessons.tip: Get the mechanics right before accusing someone. Night actions are optional, and counts like 'living others' include players who died that night, so check both before calling something a contradiction. A false 'contradiction' costs you credibility.
lessons.evidence: Erin claimed a Medic must act every night, Village players corrected her, and she was later nominated and tried. Mallory's claimed archive miscount was itself wrong, and Niaj and Alice publicly corrected it.

tips_feedback.tip: Protect every night, starting N1: target vocal analysts early, then claimed investigators. Free Standard protection stops the Katana.
tips_feedback.why: Judy protected from N1, saved Heidi on N1 and Erin on N6, and the N6 save secured the Village's 3-1 endgame.

tips_feedback.why: Alice followed it by voting Guilty on Carol and Niaj and lasted to the final day. Mallory ignored it by voting Innocent on Carol, and that record got her hanged.

tips_feedback.why: Heidi, Judy, Erin and Grace built their case on Mallory's Innocent votes on Carol and Niaj, and Mallory flipped Pharmacist.

tips_feedback.why: Carol broke this by faking Archivist while Erin was alive. The counterclaim kept her under suspicion until she was hanged, which shows the tip is sound.

tips_feedback.tip: Medic: You get no feedback on saves, so never claim you confirmed one. Say your protection is consistent with the target's survival.
tips_feedback.why: Judy consistently described her protections as having no feedback, which kept her claim credible through two trials.

tips_feedback.why: Yakuza followed it on N2 by switching off Heidi and then blocking Judy on N4 and N5 for kills. Alice ignored the same logic on N6 by attacking Erin, and Judy's protection saved her.

issues.description: Several players refer to Carol and Niaj having claimed Vanilla Villager on Day 1 (Heidi: 'Carol and Niaj's Vanilla claims are unverified'; Day 2 accusations from Heidi and Ivan), and Carol later admits 'I lied about being Vanilla'. No such claims appear anywhere in the logged Day 1 chat. Either public messages were dropped from the log or transcript, or players shared a hallucinated premise that then drove two trials.

Niaj (Mortician, 2 tokens) spent only one token on Night 1, yet on Nights 2, 3 and 4 he repeatedly told the Yakuza chat he had no Mortician token left. He never used his remaining token, including on the Night 4 kill on Frank, where cleaning was explicitly planned.
The Night 3 moderator summary says 'Erin and Niaj had no tokens to use', but Niaj still had 1 mortician token. The Night 1 summary had itself recorded '(1 left)'. This did not change any outcome.

Carol (Ballot Stuffer, 2 tokens) said in the Night 2 Yakuza chat that Heidi's 1-token audit 'conflicts with my token being spent that night' and that she had no night action. She still had 1 ballot token and could have used it; the audit was correct.

Heidi argued on Day 3 that Carol 'spent one token for Day 2 and the other for Day 3'. In fact both doubled votes (Carol's own trial and Ivan's trial) happened on Day 2 from a single token, and the Day 3 vote was not doubled. Judy echoed a similar framing.
Erin claimed a Medic must protect every night, using Niaj's N2 no-visit as a contradiction. The rules (R7) make the action optional, and other players had to correct her.

Mallory claimed Erin's N2 archive count of 9 living others was wrong because only 8 were alive. The count (11 alive at night start, 10 after Dave's death, so 9 others) was correct, and Niaj and Alice corrected it.

Mallory's last will, made public on her death, openly confirmed her own Yakuza alignment and named Alice as the Grunt and Niaj as the Mortician. This directly caused Alice's hanging and the Yakuza loss. It looks like she misunderstood that last wills are public, not ordinary strategy.
